worksheet.title: What Is a Bug?
worksheet.subtitle: Ontario Math C3.2 — read, find, and fix code
worksheet.learning_goal: I can find a bug in a loop and fix the repeat number.

parts.title: A bug is a mistake in code
text: A bug is a mistake that makes code do the wrong thing. Debugging is finding and fixing it.
Use 3 steps: say what the code SHOULD do, see what it DOES, then FIX the wrong part. Today the bug is the repeat number.

parts.caption: Debug in 3 steps: SHOULD → DOES → FIX.

parts.title: Bit should JUMP 5 times — but this is buggy
parts.note: It should be 5 jumps, but repeat 3 makes only 3. Fix the repeat number to 5.

parts.title: Find the bug
parts.prompt: Bit should CLAP 6 times. The code says repeat 4. What is wrong, and what should the repeat number be? ______

parts.title: Too many this time
parts.prompt: Bit should MOVE 4 times, but the code says repeat 7. Is that too many or too few? What should it be?

parts.title: Write the fix
parts.prompt: Bit should HOP 8 times. The code says repeat 2. Write the repeat number that fixes it:  repeat ______

parts.title: Challenge
parts.prompt: Bit should clap 6 times. The loop has TWO claps inside and says repeat 6 — so Bit claps 12! What repeat number gives exactly 6 claps? Explain.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: To debug: say what the code SHOULD do, compare it to what it DOES, and change the wrong part. A wrong repeat number is the most common loop bug.

teacher_guide.title: What Is a Bug?
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key
teacher_guide.footer_topic: 1. What Is a Bug — Teacher Guide

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Students learn the debugging method — SHOULD, DOES, FIX — and use it to fix a wrong repeat number in a loop. The method here is SHOULD → DOES → FIX: say what the code SHOULD do, run it to see what it DOES, then FIX the one thing that is wrong. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start
parts.text: No computer needed — the worksheet shows the code and what Bit should do. Optional: a Scratch-style app (for the block loops) or a free Python-turtle playground (for the shapes) to run the code — you only press Run.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 30 minutes)
text: 1. Show it (you do). Say what Bit SHOULD do (clap 6 times), run the loop to see what it DOES (claps 4), then FIX the repeat number.
2. Do one together. Exercise 1 — change repeat 4 to repeat 6.
3. Let them work. Students fix too-many and too-few repeats (Ex 2–3), and separate total from repeat count when two blocks are inside (Ex 4).

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — repeat 6 (repeat 4 is too few). Exercise 2 — too many; should be repeat 4.
Exercise 3 — repeat 8. Exercise 4 (challenge) — repeat 3 (2 claps × 3 = 6); repeat 6 would give 12.

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: skipping the SHOULD step. Name the goal first, then compare.
Make it easier: count the goal, count what the loop does, and find the difference.
Make it harder: ask the repeat number when three blocks are inside and Bit should do 9.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events.
In plain terms: students write and run step-by-step instructions — including a "repeat" instruction — to make something happen.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read instructions, find what is wrong, fix it, and explain what the change did.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child uses SHOULD–DOES–FIX to set the repeat number so the loop matches the goal.
